subject: chemistry
title: Empirical and molecular formulae
key_idea: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. The molecular formula is the actual number of atoms. Find the empirical formula from masses or percentages, then scale it up using the relative molecular mass.

blocks.text: Two formulae describe the same compound in different ways. This section covers what each one shows and how they are related.

items.meaning: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
The actual number and type of atoms of each element in one molecule.

items: The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.
For some compounds the two are the same, such as H₂O and CH₄.
Ionic compounds are only given an empirical formula, because they have no molecules.
You can also read both formulae from a structural, displayed or skeletal formula by counting the atoms.
Empirical formula: simplest ratio.
Molecular formula: actual atoms in one molecule.
Molecular formula = n × empirical formula.

blocks.text: Experimental data gives masses or percentages by mass. Convert them to moles, then to a whole-number ratio.

items.text: A percentage by mass can be treated as the mass in 100 g.
This gives the amount in moles of each element.
Divide every amount by the smallest amount.
If a ratio is 1.5, multiply everything by 2. If it is 1.33, multiply by 3.

blocks.text: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass.

diagram.alt: Put the steps for finding an empirical formula in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps for finding an empirical formula in order.
steps: Write the mass (or percentage) of each element
Divide each mass by its molar mass to get moles
Divide every amount by the smallest amount
Multiply to get whole numbers if needed

items: Convert mass to moles, then to a ratio.
A ratio such as 1.5 must be multiplied up to whole numbers.
Do not round 1.33 or 1.5 to a whole number.

blocks.text: The molecular formula needs the relative molecular mass as well as the empirical formula.

items.text: The molecular formula is 6 × CH₂O = C₆H₁₂O₆.

items: Mᵣ can come from a mass spectrum or from a gas measurement.
For a gas or volatile liquid, use pV = nRT to find the amount, then Mᵣ = mass ÷ amount.

items.meaning: A crystal that contains water as part of its structure.
A substance containing no water of crystallisation.
Water molecules bonded into the crystal structure of a salt, shown after a dot: CuSO₄·5H₂O.

blocks.text: Heat the salt to drive off the water. The mass lost is the water. Treat the water as one of the 'elements' in the ratio.

items.text: 4.99 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate loses 1.80 g on heating. Anhydrous CuSO₄ left: 3.19 g.
0.100 ÷ 0.0200 = 5, so x = 5 and the formula is CuSO₄·5H₂O.

items: Mᵣ ÷ empirical formula mass gives the multiplier.
Hydrated salts: find the ratio of salt to water in moles.
Water of crystallisation is written after a dot.

checks.q: Define the terms empirical formula and molecular formula.
checks.a: Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule.

checks.q: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon by mass and has Mᵣ = 56.0. Find its empirical and molecular formulae.
checks.a: Hydrogen = 14.3%. C: 85.7 ÷ 12.0 = 7.14; H: 14.3 ÷ 1.0 = 14.3. Ratio 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH₂ (mass 14.0). 56.0 ÷ 14.0 = 4, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈.

checks.q: 6.15 g of hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄·xH₂O, gives 3.01 g of anhydrous MgSO₄ on heating. Find x. (Mᵣ of MgSO₄ = 120.4; H₂O = 18.0.)

items: You must use the terms, but you are not asked to give formal definitions of empirical and molecular formula.
Calculate empirical formulae from elemental analysis data, such as the masses of CO₂ and H₂O formed on burning a compound.
Calculate the formula of a hydrated salt from percentage composition, mass composition or experimental results.
Use experimental data to calculate empirical formulae, from masses or percentage composition by mass.
Calculate molecular formulae using pV = nRT for gases and volatile liquids: find n, then Mᵣ = mass ÷ n.
Calculate empirical formula from composition by mass or percentage by mass.
Calculate molecular formula from the empirical formula and the relative molecular mass.
Deduce the molecular and empirical formula of an organic compound from its structural, displayed or skeletal formula.
In a skeletal formula, each line end or corner is a carbon atom. Add hydrogen atoms until each carbon has four bonds.
Example: cyclohexane drawn as a hexagon is C₆H₁₂, with empirical formula CH₂.
